Electric current as the rate of charge flow; the ampere as one coulomb per second; I = dQ/dt

claims.claim: Since 20 May 2019 the ampere is defined by fixing the elementary charge e at exactly 1.602 176 634 x 10^-19 coulomb, where the coulomb equals the ampere second; one ampere therefore corresponds to the flow of 1/(1.602 176 634 x 10^-19) elementary charges per second, about 6.2415 x 10^18 per second.
Electric current is the rate at which charge flows: I_avg = delta_Q / delta_t and I = dQ/dt, and one ampere is one coulomb per second.

Conventional current is defined as flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, a convention inherited from Franklin-era charge conventions, even though in a metal the moving carriers are electrons drifting in the opposite direction.

Drift velocity is the average velocity of the free charges and satisfies I = n q A v_d; in a 12-gauge copper wire carrying 20.0 A the drift speed is about 4.54 x 10^-4 m/s, while electrical signals travel on the order of 10^8 m/s, a significant fraction of the speed of light.

Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge, V = U/q, and potential difference is delta_V = delta_U/q, measured in volts where 1 V = 1 J/C; the point chosen as zero volts is arbitrary, so only differences of potential carry physical meaning.
In coherent SI units the coulomb is A s, the volt is W/A = kg m^2 s^-3 A^-1, the ohm is V/A = kg m^2 s^-3 A^-2, and the siemens is A/V = kg^-1 m^-2 s^3 A^2.

Resistivity rho is a property of the material and is the reciprocal of conductivity; the resistance of a uniform conductor of length L and cross-sectional area A is R = rho L / A, and one ohm equals one volt per ampere.

At 20.00 degrees Celsius the resistivity of copper is about 1.68 x 10^-8 ohm metre and that of aluminium about 2.65 x 10^-8 ohm metre; resistivity varies with temperature approximately as rho = rho_0 [1 + alpha (T - T_0)], with alpha about 0.0039 per degree Celsius for both copper and aluminium.

Materials span an enormous resistivity range: conductors around 10^-8 to 10^-7 ohm metre, semiconductors roughly 10^-5 to 10^3 ohm metre, and insulators above about 10^11 ohm metre (glass 10^9 to 10^14, hard rubber 10^13 to 10^16 ohm metre).

Electromotive force is not a force but the work done per unit charge by a source, measured in volts; an ideal source holds its terminal voltage constant, while a real source has internal resistance r so that the terminal voltage is V_terminal = emf - I r and falls as the current rises.

In U.S. workplace electrical regulation, 'ground' means a conducting connection, intentional or accidental, between an electric circuit or equipment and the earth or to some conducting body that serves in place of the earth; a conducting body may therefore stand in for the earth as the reference.

Live parts to which an employee may be exposed must be deenergized before work on or near them unless the employer can demonstrate that deenergizing introduces additional or increased hazards or is infeasible, and only qualified persons may work on circuit parts that have not been deenergized.

A copper conductor 30.0 m long with a 2.00 mm diameter has cross-sectional area 3.1416 x 10^-6 m^2 and resistance 0.160 ohm at 20.00 degrees Celsius; the same geometry in aluminium gives 0.253 ohm, and heating the copper conductor to 75 degrees Celsius raises its resistance to about 0.19 ohm.
Because resistance varies as 1/A and A varies as the square of the diameter, halving the diameter of a round conductor quadruples its resistance.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the ampere or the coulomb is the 'more fundamental' unit.
positions: Historically the ampere was an SI base unit defined by a force between conductors, and the coulomb was derived from it.
Since 2019 the SI defines the ampere by fixing the elementary charge, so charge is the quantity carrying the exact defining value while the ampere remains a base unit by convention.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches charge as the physically underlying quantity and states that the ampere remains an SI base unit whose definition now rests on an exactly fixed elementary charge, per the SI Brochure and NIST SP 330. The base/derived split is described as a retained convention rather than a claim about physics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reported temperature coefficient of copper varies slightly across references (values near 0.0039 to 0.0043 per degree Celsius appear in different tables, depending on purity and reference temperature).
positions: OpenStax University Physics Volume 2 Table 9.1 lists alpha = 0.0039 per degree Celsius for copper at T_0 = 20.00 degrees Celsius.
Other handbooks list slightly higher values for annealed commercial copper.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the single sourced value 0.0039 per degree Celsius, states the reference temperature, calls the result approximate, and reports the heated resistance to two significant figures because alpha carries only two.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no electrical content at all: it described 'voltage, current, and resistance' as a generic organizing concept, a 'label on a toolbox drawer', with no charge, no units, no equations and no sources.
The draft's vocabulary block defined the topic in terms of itself ('a foundational Engineering Fundamentals concept covered in this lesson'), which is circular and unverifiable.
The draft's worked example described a student reading a scenario rather than performing any engineering calculation.
The draft's question bank tested study technique rather than any electrical fact.
The draft carried no analogy limits, which this subject's source map requires.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire lesson with sourced electrical content anchored on charge, current, voltage and resistance.
Added the post-2019 SI basis: the ampere defined by an exactly fixed elementary charge, and the coulomb, volt, ohm and siemens expressed in SI base units.
Added the conventional-current versus electron-drift confusion to Common Mistakes, as the unit's most persistent beginner error.
Added drift velocity versus signal speed with sourced magnitudes, correctly explained as a field effect rather than fast-moving electrons.
Added the requirement that voltage is stated between two points, or relative to a named reference node.
Added the water analogy together with an explicit statement of where it fails, as required by the subject source map.
Added an explicit educational-scope and electrical-safety statement citing the governing OSHA requirements.
Executed every published number in Bash (python3) before writing it, carrying units at each step.
